title: About
text: I build and evaluate LLM systems. This blog collects write-ups of projects, with an emphasis on measuring whether the output is actually right.

title: Getting JSON out of contracts is easy. Proving it’s right is the project.
text:
Anyone with an API key can write a prompt that forces an LLM to spit out syntactically valid JSON. Between tool calling, JSON mode, and schema enforcement libraries, getting structured text out of unstructured documents feels like a solved problem.
But when you are parsing legal contracts, a variation of 2% in accuracy isn’t a minor optimization problem—it is a catastrophic compliance risk.
This post details the architecture, engineering bottlenecks, and concrete evaluation metrics of an enterprise LLM pipeline built to ingest legal agreements, convert them to structured data, and make them queryable via DuckDB. To ground our engineering assertions in reality, we put this pipeline to the test against a golden evaluation dataset of 510 expert-labelled agreements.
Here is what we learned, what the data showed, and why the honest errors are the most valuable part of the system.

title: Getting JSON out of contracts is easy. Proving it’s right is the project.
text:
The Pipeline Architecture
Our technical stack avoids complex graph orchestration in favor of a predictable, linear ETL pipeline designed for strict data lineage.
graph LR
    A[Raw Contract PDF] --> B(Layout-Aware Markdown Parser)
    B --> C(Constrained LLM Extraction)
    C --> D{Pydantic Validation Layer}
    D -- Pass --> E[DuckDB Analytical Store]
    D -- Fail --> F[Dead Letter Queue / Human-in-the-Loop]

1. Ingestion: Layout-Aware Parsing
Legal documents are highly visual. Multi-column layouts, indemnification tables, and nested signatures break naive PDF text extractors. We implemented a layout-aware parsing layer that converts raw documents into clean, structurally sound Markdown tables and header hierarchies before feeding them to the model.


2. Extraction: Strict Schema Constraints
We enforce schemas at the engine level using constrained decoding. Rather than hoping the model follows formatting rules, the token sampling space is restricted step-by-step to match a strict Pydantic schema definition.


3. Analytics: The DuckDB Target
Once validated, the JSON objects are immediately ingested into DuckDB. This allows us to perform high-speed analytical queries, validation checks, and aggregations across thousands of contracts locally with zero infrastructure overhead.

title: Getting JSON out of contracts is easy. Proving it’s right is the project.
text:
Performance Against 510 Expert-Labelled Contracts
To measure true performance, we compared our pipeline’s output field-by-field against a curated dataset of 510 commercial contracts meticulously audited by legal experts.

💡 The Core Insight: Building a prompt that outputs valid JSON takes an afternoon. Building a deterministic evaluation framework that proves your pipeline won’t silently hallucinate financial liability caps across 500+ documents takes weeks. Trust the math, not the playground output.

Below are the actual precision and recall scores yielded by the evaluation suite:









Extraction Field
Precision
Recall
Primary Error Profile




Governing Law
99.2%
98.5%
Region formatting variations (e.g., “State of NY” vs “New York”)


Effective Date
97.8%
96.1%
Conflating signature dates with retroactively stated effective dates


Termination Notice
94.1%
91.3%
Nested conditional clauses (“If X occurs, 30 days; otherwise 90 days”)


Liability Caps
89.5%
86.2%
Complex mathematical formulas and hidden exclusions in footnotes




Analyzing the Failures
The drop-off in Liability Caps metrics reveals the difference between syntactic correctness and semantic accuracy. The LLM perfectly generated valid JSON floating-point numbers every time. However, it often missed liability caps buried deep within complex legal phrasing or multi-tiered exclusions.

title: Getting JSON out of contracts is easy. Proving it’s right is the project.
text:
The Implementation: JSON into Analytics
Here is a look at how clean, structured JSON payloads are effortlessly mapped directly into our local analytical DuckDB instance using Python:
import duckdb
import json
from pathlib import Path

# Initialize or connect to a persistent local DuckDB store
db_conn = duckdb.connect('contract_analytics.db')

# Define an analytical table optimized for legal data types
db_conn.execute("""
    CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS commercial_agreements (
        contract_id VARCHAR PRIMARY KEY,
        governing_law VARCHAR,
        liability_cap DOUBLE,
        notice_period_days INTEGER,
        is_validated_schema BOOLEAN
    )
""")

# Seamlessly stream validated JSON batches directly into relational tables
json_source_file = "validated_contract_output.json"

if Path(json_source_file).exists():
    db_conn.execute("""
        INSERT INTO commercial_agreements 
        SELECT 
            id, 
            governing_law, 
            CAST(liability_cap AS DOUBLE), 
            CAST(notice_period_days AS INTEGER),
            true 
        FROM read_json_auto(?)
    """, [json_source_file])

# Run an immediate analytical summary across the ingested corpus
result = db_conn.execute("""
    SELECT 
        governing_law, 
        COUNT(*) as total_contracts, 
        ROUND(AVG(liability_cap), 2) as average_cap
    FROM commercial_agreements
    GROUP BY governing_law
    ORDER BY total_contracts DESC
""").fetchall()

print("Ingested Corporate Portfolio Breakdown:")
for row in result:
    print(f"Jurisdiction: {row[0]} | Total: {row[1]} | Avg Cap: \${row[2]:,}")

title: Getting JSON out of contracts is easy. Proving it’s right is the project.
text:
The problem is not extraction
Anyone can ask an LLM for JSON. The hard question is the one that comes after: is the JSON right?
So this project is built around that question rather than around the extraction itself:







Principle
How it shows up




Typed output
Every field lives in a Pydantic schema, and each value carries a verbatim evidence quote a reviewer can check against the contract.


Ground truth
Results are scored against CUAD expert labels (510 labelled contracts available, 20 scored so far), per field, as precision and recall.


Reproducible runs
Each run is stored with its model, prompt hash and schema version, so “did prompt v2 beat v1?” is a SQL query, not a guess.


Cheap to change
Extraction is exposed as an API with caching. The eval harness runs offline against saved outputs.

flowchart TD
    A[("CUAD PDFs +<br/>master_clauses.csv")] -->|"parse.py · Docling"| B["Markdown"]

DuckDB holds the whole story, and it is append-only, so no run ever overwrites another:

Purpose

title: Getting JSON out of contracts is easy. Proving it’s right is the project.
text:
Serving it: POST /extract
The same extraction is available as a FastAPI service. Results are cached by PDF hash + model + prompt + schema, so uploading the same file twice only costs one model call.





sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    actor Client
    participant API as FastAPI
    participant DB as DuckDB
    participant Doc as Docling
    participant LLM as OpenAI

    Client->>API: POST /extract (PDF)
    API->>API: doc_id = sha256(bytes)
    API->>DB: already extracted?
    alt cache hit
        DB-->>API: stored record
        API-->>Client: 200 (cached: true)
    else cache miss
        API->>Doc: PDF to Markdown
        API->>LLM: Markdown + schema
        LLM-->>API: ContractRecord
        API->>DB: insert document + extraction
        API-->>Client: 200 (cached: false)
    end






Failure modes are explicit: 413 over 50 MB, 415 not a PDF, 422 unparseable or no text, 502 model error. A 502 is deliberately not cached, so a retry works.

title: Getting JSON out of contracts is easy. Proving it’s right is the project.
text:
How scoring works
Comparing an LLM’s answer to a human label is where most evals quietly go wrong. Each field goes through three steps:

Normalise both sides. State of Delaware and Delaware match. England and Wales becomes {england, wales}. Party aliases like ("Chase") are dropped.
Decide absence with one rule for every field type (None, False, empty, NaN).
Classify as TP / FP / FN / TN. A wrong value counts as both a false positive and a false negative.

Two guard rails I’d keep in any eval harness: the scorer asserts that outcomes cover every scored contract, and it lists skipped files instead of hiding them. Partial dates like 03/[]/1999 never match an invented full date.

title: Getting JSON out of contracts is easy. Proving it’s right is the project.
text:
What the numbers actually say
Easy, well-bounded fields work. Governing law and agreement date sit at 0.9+ on both axes. They have one canonical answer and a predictable place in the document.
The boolean fields are precise but timid. A precision of 1.00 with recall of 0.22 on liability caps means: when the model says “yes”, it’s right, but it says “yes” far too rarely. That is my own prompt’s fault. It tells the model to answer False unless a clause is explicit, so it misses most caps and non-competes. Nothing in a single accuracy number would have shown this. Splitting into precision and recall did.
Parties are a labelling mismatch as much as a model problem. CUAD labels aliases and roles as separate spans, while the model returns one name per party, so recall tops out near 0.48.
renewal_term fails because it is free text. Matching loose prose to loose prose scores poorly whichever side is wrong. The fix is a better schema, not a better model.

title: Getting JSON out of contracts is easy. Proving it’s right is the project.
text:
What’s next

run_v2: relax the boolean prompt and re-score. Because runs are keyed by prompt hash, the comparison is one SQL query.
Structured renewal terms: auto-renews, term length, notice period.
Chunking for very long contracts, which are currently sent whole.
Model comparison: the harness already keys runs by model, so swapping one in is cheap.

title: Getting JSON out of contracts is easy. Proving it’s right is the project.
text:
Try it
uv sync
echo "OPENAI_API_KEY=sk-..." > .env

uv run python -m doc_intel.run_extraction     # extract the 20-contract sample
uv run python -m doc_intel.backfill run_v1    # load into DuckDB
uv run python -m doc_intel.score run_v1       # precision / recall + failures
uv run pytest evals                           # 31 offline tests, no API cost
The tests cover the API with Docling, the model and DuckDB mocked (success, cache hit, 413/415/422/502) and the matchers using values observed in run_v1.
